topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Prove that the intersection of any finite collection of open sets in $\mathbb{R}$ is open.
concept_tested: Finite Intersection of Open Sets in $\mathbb{R}$
approach: Let $x \in \bigcap_{k=1}^m G_k$, find open intervals $(x-\epsilon_k, x+\epsilon_k) \subseteq G_k$, and take $\epsilon = \min \epsilon_k > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Setup
solution_steps.math: G = \bigcap_{k=1}^m G_k, \quad x \in G \implies x \in G_k \quad \forall k \in \{1, 2, \dots, m\}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x$ belongs to the intersection, it belongs to each individual open set $G_k$.

solution_steps.title: Openness of Each $G_k$
solution_steps.math: \forall k \in \{1, \dots, m\}, \; \exists \epsilon_k > 0 \text{ such that } V_{\epsilon_k}(x) = (x - \epsilon_k, x + \epsilon_k) \subseteq G_k
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of open sets in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Taking Minimum Radius
solution_steps.math: \epsilon = \min\{\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2, \dots, \epsilon_m\} > 0 \implies V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq V_{\epsilon_k}(x) \subseteq G_k \; (\forall k) \implies V_\epsilon(x) \subseteq \bigcap_{k=1}^m G_k = G
solution_steps.explanation: The minimum of finitely many strictly positive real numbers is strictly positive. Hence $G$ is open.

final_answer: The intersection of any finite collection of open sets is open because $\epsilon = \min_{1 \le k \le m} \epsilon_k > 0$.
exam_tip: Emphasize why this fails for infinite intersections: the infimum of infinitely many positive numbers can be 0 (e.g. $\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1/n) = \{0\}$, which is not open).

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State the definition of uniform convergence of a sequence of functions.
concept_tested: Definition of Uniform Convergence of Sequence of Functions
approach: State the $\epsilon-K$ definition where $K$ depends solely on $\epsilon$, not on $x$.

solution_steps.title: Formal Definition
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \text{ on } A \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K(\epsilon) \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } \forall n \ge K, \; \forall x \in A, \; |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence of functions $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to $f$ on a set $A$ if the rate of convergence is uniform across all points $x \in A$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Norm Equivalent
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \|f_n - f\|_A = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sup_{x \in A} |f_n(x) - f(x)| = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Uniform convergence is equivalent to convergence in the uniform (supremum) norm.

final_answer: $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $A$ if $\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$ and all $x \in A$.
exam_tip: Write the quantifiers in order: '$\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K \in \mathbb{N}, \forall n \ge K, \forall x \in A$'. Placing $\forall x$ before $\exists K$ gives pointwise convergence!

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Write the difference between pointwise convergence and uniform convergence.
concept_tested: Pointwise vs Uniform Convergence
approach: Contrast the quantifier dependencies: $K(\epsilon, x)$ vs $K(\epsilon)$, and preservation of continuity.

solution_steps.title: Quantifier Dependency
solution_steps.math: \text{Pointwise: } K = K(\epsilon, x); \qquad \text{Uniform: } K = K(\epsilon) \text{ (independent of } x)
solution_steps.explanation: In pointwise convergence, different points $x$ can require different numbers of terms to get within $\epsilon$. In uniform convergence, a single $K$ works simultaneously for all points in the domain.

solution_steps.title: Property Preservation
solution_steps.math: \text{Uniform convergence preserves continuity and integrates term-by-term; pointwise convergence does not.}
solution_steps.explanation: Pointwise limits of continuous functions can be discontinuous (e.g., $x^n$ on $[0, 1]$).

final_answer: Pointwise: $K$ depends on both $\epsilon$ and $x$. Uniform: $K$ depends only on $\epsilon$, holding simultaneously for all $x \in A$. Uniform convergence guarantees the limit of continuous functions is continuous.
exam_tip: A two-column comparison table is the cleanest way to present this answer in an exam.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence of infinite series of functions.
concept_tested: Weierstrass M-Test
approach: State hypotheses $|f_n(x)| \le M_n$ and $\sum M_n < \infty$, and the conclusion of uniform and absolute convergence.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: |f_n(x)| \le M_n \quad \forall x \in A, \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n < \infty
solution_steps.explanation: If each function $f_n$ is bounded on $A$ by a constant $M_n$, and the numerical series $\sum M_n$ converges.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x) \text{ converges absolutely and uniformly on } A
solution_steps.explanation: The series of functions converges uniformly to a function $S(x)$ on $A$.

final_answer: If $|f_n(x)| \le M_n$ for all $x \in A$ and $\sum M_n$ converges, then $\sum f_n$ converges uniformly and absolutely on $A$.
exam_tip: Remember that $M_n$ must be constants independent of $x$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define the radius of convergence of a power series.
concept_tested: Radius of Convergence of Power Series
approach: Define $R$ via Cauchy-Hadamard formula $1/R = \limsup |a_n|^{1/n}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: R = \sup\{r \ge 0 : \sum a_n r^n \text{ converges}\} \in [0, \infty]
solution_steps.explanation: The radius of convergence $R$ is the non-negative number (or $\infty$) such that $\sum a_n (x-c)^n$ converges for $|x-c| < R$ and diverges for $|x-c| > R$.

solution_steps.title: Cauchy-Hadamard Formula
solution_steps.math: \frac{1}{R} = \limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n|^{1/n} \quad (\text{or } \frac{1}{R} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| \text{ when it exists})
solution_steps.explanation: Standard computational formulas.

final_answer: The radius of convergence $R$ is defined by $\frac{1}{R} = \limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n|^{1/n}$ (with $R=0$ if $\limsup = \infty$, and $R=\infty$ if $\limsup = 0$).
exam_tip: Mention that convergence at the boundary points $|x - c| = R$ must be tested separately.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Find the radius of convergence of the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n! x^n$.
concept_tested: Radius of Convergence Calculation
approach: Apply Ratio Test to coefficients $a_n = n!$.

solution_steps.title: Ratio of Coefficients
solution_steps.math: \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{(n+1)!}{n!} = n + 1
solution_steps.explanation: Compute consecutive coefficient ratio.

solution_steps.title: Take Limit
solution_steps.math: L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} (n+1) = +\infty
solution_steps.explanation: The ratio diverges to $+\infty$.

solution_steps.title: Radius of Convergence
solution_steps.math: R = \frac{1}{L} = \frac{1}{\infty} = 0
solution_steps.explanation: The series converges only at $x = 0$.

final_answer: The radius of convergence is $R = 0$.
exam_tip: $R = 0$ means the series converges only at the single point $x = 0$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define pointwise convergence of a sequence of functions.
concept_tested: Pointwise Convergence of Sequence of Functions
approach: State the definition that for every fixed $x_0 \in A$, the real sequence $(f_n(x_0))$ converges to $f(x_0)$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: f_n \to f \text{ pointwise on } A \iff \forall x \in A, \; \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently: $\forall x \in A, \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists K(x, \epsilon) \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n \ge K \implies |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \epsilon$.

final_answer: $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to $f$ on $A$ if for each fixed $x \in A$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)$.
exam_tip: Stress that $K$ is allowed to vary with $x$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Write the power series expansion of $e^x$ and find its interval of convergence.
concept_tested: Taylor / Power Series for $e^x$
approach: Write $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$ and apply Ratio Test to find $R = \infty$.

solution_steps.title: Power Series Expansion
solution_steps.math: e^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^3}{3!} + \dots
solution_steps.explanation: Maclaurin series for $e^x$.

solution_steps.title: Radius of Convergence
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} \left|\frac{x^{n+1}/(n+1)!}{x^n/n!}\right| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{|x|}{n+1} = 0 < 1 \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Ratio Test, the series converges for every real number $x$, so $R = \infty$.

final_answer: Expansion: $e^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$. Interval of convergence: $(-\infty, \infty) = \mathbb{R}$.
exam_tip: State both the radius of convergence $R = \infty$ and the interval of convergence $(-\infty, \infty)$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Determine the limit of sequence $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0, 1]$ as $n \to \infty$.
concept_tested: Pointwise Limit of $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0, 1]$
approach: Analyze cases $x \in [0, 1)$ and $x = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Case $0 \le x < 1$
solution_steps.math: |x| < 1 \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} x^n = 0
solution_steps.explanation: Standard geometric sequence limit.

solution_steps.title: Case $x = 1$
solution_steps.math: x = 1 \implies f_n(1) = 1^n = 1 \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(1) = 1
solution_steps.explanation: Constant sequence of 1s.

final_answer: $f(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty} x^n = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \le x < 1 \\ 1, & x = 1 \end{cases}$.
exam_tip: Note that the limit function is discontinuous at $x = 1$, which proves the convergence is not uniform on $[0, 1]$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State Abel's limit theorem for power series.
concept_tested: Abel's Limit Theorem for Power Series
approach: State that if a power series converges at an endpoint, the sum function is continuous up to that endpoint.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n R^n \text{ converges} \implies \lim_{x \to R^-} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n R^n
solution_steps.explanation: If a real power series $\sum a_n x^n$ with radius of convergence $R$ converges at $x = R$, then the sum function $f(x)$ is continuous from the left at $x = R$.

final_answer: If $\sum a_n R^n$ converges, then $f(x) = \sum a_n x^n$ is continuous on $[0, R]$, so $\lim_{x \to R^-} f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n R^n$.
exam_tip: A classic application of Abel's Theorem is evaluating the alternating harmonic series: $\ln(2) = 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - \dots$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State the Taylor series theorem for real functions.
concept_tested: Taylor's Theorem with Remainder
approach: State Taylor's Theorem with Lagrange form of the remainder.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.explanation: If $f$ has $n+1$ derivatives on an interval containing $x_0$ and $x$.

solution_steps.title: Lagrange Form of Remainder
solution_steps.math: R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!} (x - x_0)^{n+1} \quad \text{for some } c \text{ strictly between } x_0 \text{ and } x
solution_steps.explanation: The error term resembles the next term in the series evaluated at an intermediate point $c$.

final_answer: $f(x) = P_n(x) + R_n(x)$ where $R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-x_0)^{n+1}$ for some $c$ between $x_0$ and $x$.
exam_tip: Note that for $n = 0$, Taylor's theorem reduces directly to the Mean Value Theorem.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Verify if the function $f(x) = |x|$ is differentiable at $x=0$.
concept_tested: Differentiability of Absolute Value Function at Origin
approach: Compute left-hand and right-hand limits of the difference quotient at $x = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Difference Quotient at 0
solution_steps.explanation: Evaluating the difference quotient.

solution_steps.title: Right-hand Derivative
solution_steps.explanation: Since $h > 0 \implies |h| = h$.

solution_steps.title: Left-hand Derivative
solution_steps.explanation: Since $h < 0 \implies |h| = -h$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: f'_+(0) = 1 \ne -1 = f'_-(0) \implies f'(0) \text{ does not exist}
solution_steps.explanation: The two one-sided derivatives disagree.

final_answer: $f(x) = |x|$ is NOT differentiable at $x = 0$ because the right derivative is $+1$ while the left derivative is $-1$.
exam_tip: Note that $f(x) = |x|$ is continuous everywhere on $\mathbb{R}$ despite failing to be differentiable at 0.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define the interval of convergence of a power series.
concept_tested: Interval of Convergence of a Power Series
approach: Define interval $I$ centered at $c$ of radius $R$, including any convergent boundary endpoints.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: I = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n (x - c)^n \text{ converges}\}
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all real points $x$ for which the power series converges.

solution_steps.title: Structure
solution_steps.math: (c - R, c + R) \subseteq I \subseteq [c - R, c + R]
solution_steps.explanation: It is always an interval centered at $c$. It can be open, closed, or half-open depending on convergence at endpoints $c \pm R$.

final_answer: The interval of convergence is the set of all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ where the power series converges. It has one of the four forms: $(c-R, c+R)$, $[c-R, c+R)$, $(c-R, c+R]$, or $[c-R, c+R]$.
exam_tip: Emphasize that the interval of convergence always includes the interior $(c-R, c+R)$, but endpoints require independent investigation.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State the definition of a metric space and give an example of a metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$.
concept_tested: Definition of Metric Space and Example on $\mathbb{R}^2$
approach: State the 4 metric axioms (non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, triangle inequality) and give Euclidean or Taxicab metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

solution_steps.title: Metric Space Definition
solution_steps.math: d: X \times X \to \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } (1) \, d(x,y) \ge 0, \; (2) \, d(x,y)=0 \iff x=y, \; (3) \, d(x,y)=d(y,x), \; (4) \, d(x,z) \le d(x,y)+d(y,z)
solution_steps.explanation: A set $X$ equipped with a function $d$ satisfying these four axioms is a metric space $(X, d)$.

solution_steps.title: Example on $\mathbb{R}^2$
solution_steps.math: d_2((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2} \quad (\text{Euclidean Metric})
solution_steps.explanation: Or the Taxicab (Manhattan) metric: $d_1((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)) = |x_1 - x_2| + |y_1 - y_2|$.

final_answer: A metric space is a pair $(X, d)$ satisfying non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, and triangle inequality. Example on $\mathbb{R}^2$: Euclidean metric $d(x, y) = \sqrt{(x_1-y_1)^2 + (x_2-y_2)^2}$.
exam_tip: Writing out all 4 axioms clearly guarantees full credit.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define open and closed balls in a metric space.
concept_tested: Open and Closed Balls in Metric Space
approach: Define $B(x_0, r)$ using strict inequality and $\overline{B}(x_0, r)$ using non-strict inequality.

solution_steps.title: Open Ball
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all points in $X$ whose metric distance from center $x_0$ is strictly less than radius $r > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Closed Ball
solution_steps.math: \overline{B}(x_0, r) = \overline{B}_r(x_0) = \{x \in X : d(x, x_0) \le r\}
solution_steps.explanation: The set of all points whose distance from $x_0$ is less than or equal to $r$.

final_answer: Open ball: $B(x_0, r) = \{x \in X : d(x, x_0) < r\}$. Closed ball: $\overline{B}(x_0, r) = \{x \in X : d(x, x_0) \le r\}$.
exam_tip: Notice that $r$ must be strictly positive ($r > 0$).

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Verify whether $d(x, y) = |x-y|$ defines a metric on the set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$.
concept_tested: Verification of Absolute Value Metric on $\mathbb{R}$
approach: Verify the four metric axioms for $d(x, y) = |x - y|$.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 1: Non-negativity
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = |x - y| \ge 0 \quad \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of absolute value.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 2: Identity of Indiscernibles
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = 0 \iff |x - y| = 0 \iff x - y = 0 \iff x = y
solution_steps.explanation: The absolute value is zero if and only if the argument is zero.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 3: Symmetry
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|-u| = |u|$.

solution_steps.title: Axiom 4: Triangle Inequality
solution_steps.explanation: By the standard triangle inequality for real numbers.

final_answer: Yes, $d(x, y) = |x - y|$ satisfies all four axioms and is the standard metric on $\mathbb{R}$.
exam_tip: List and verify each of the 4 axioms in numbered order.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define a complete metric space. Is the set of rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ complete under the standard metric?
concept_tested: Complete Metric Space & Incompleteness of $\mathbb{Q}$
approach: Define complete metric space; give counterexample sequence of rationals converging to an irrational.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Complete Metric Space
solution_steps.math: (X, d) \text{ is complete} \iff \text{every Cauchy sequence in } X \text{ converges to a limit in } X
solution_steps.explanation: A metric space is complete if there are no 'missing points'.

solution_steps.title: Incompleteness of $\mathbb{Q}$
solution_steps.math: x_1 = 1, \quad x_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x_n + \frac{2}{x_n}\right) \implies x_n \in \mathbb{Q} \; \forall n
solution_steps.explanation: The sequence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence of rational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Limit does not belong to $\mathbb{Q}$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = \sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$, the Cauchy sequence does not converge within $(\mathbb{Q}, |\cdot|)$.

final_answer: A metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence in it converges to a point in the space. $\mathbb{Q}$ is NOT complete because sequences of rationals converging to $\sqrt{2}$ are Cauchy but have no limit in $\mathbb{Q}$.
exam_tip: State that $\mathbb{R}$ is the metric completion of $\mathbb{Q}$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State the Heine-Borel Theorem for the real line $\mathbb{R}$.
concept_tested: Heine-Borel Theorem for $\mathbb{R}$
approach: State the characterization of compactness in Euclidean space: closed and bounded.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: K \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ is compact} \iff K \text{ is closed and bounded}
solution_steps.explanation: A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has the property that every open cover has a finite subcover if and only if it is closed and bounded.

final_answer: A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^n$) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
exam_tip: Heine-Borel fails in general infinite-dimensional metric spaces (where closed and bounded does not imply compact).

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State the Banach Fixed Point Theorem.
concept_tested: Banach Fixed Point Theorem (Contraction Mapping Principle)
approach: State hypotheses: complete metric space, contraction mapping with $k < 1$; conclude unique fixed point.

solution_steps.title: Hypotheses
solution_steps.math: (X, d) \text{ complete metric space}, \quad T: X \to X \text{ s.t. } d(T(x), T(y)) \le k d(x, y) \quad (0 \le k < 1)
solution_steps.explanation: $T$ is a contraction mapping on a complete metric space.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \exists! x^* \in X \text{ such that } T(x^*) = x^*, \quad x^* = \lim_{n \to \infty} T^n(x_0) \; \forall x_0 \in X
solution_steps.explanation: There exists a unique fixed point $x^*$, and Picard iteration converges to $x^*$ from any starting point.

final_answer: If $(X, d)$ is a complete metric space and $T: X \to X$ is a contraction ($d(Tx, Ty) \le k d(x, y)$ with $k < 1$), then $T$ has a unique fixed point $x^* \in X$.
exam_tip: State both the existence and uniqueness of the fixed point, and that $k$ must be strictly less than 1.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define the boundary of a subset $A$ in a metric space.
concept_tested: Boundary of a Subset in Metric Space
approach: Define $\partial A = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}$ or via neighborhoods intersecting both $A$ and $A^c$.

solution_steps.title: Definition via Balls
solution_steps.math: x \in \partial A \iff \forall r > 0, \; B(x, r) \cap A \ne \emptyset \quad \text{and} \quad B(x, r) \cap (X \setminus A) \ne \emptyset
solution_steps.explanation: A point $x$ is in the boundary of $A$ if every open ball centered at $x$ contains at least one point of $A$ and at least one point not in $A$.

solution_steps.title: Topological Characterization
solution_steps.math: \partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}
solution_steps.explanation: The boundary equals the closure minus the interior.

final_answer: The boundary $\partial A$ is the set of points whose every neighborhood intersects both $A$ and $X \setminus A$: $\partial A = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}$.
exam_tip: Example: In $\mathbb{R}$, $\partial(0, 1) = \{0, 1\}$ and $\partial \mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{R}$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define the closure of a set $A$ in a metric space.
concept_tested: Closure of a Set in a Metric Space
approach: Define $\overline{A}$ as $A \cup A'$ (set plus limit points) or intersection of all closed supersets.

solution_steps.title: Definition via Limit Points
solution_steps.math: \overline{A} = A \cup A'
solution_steps.explanation: The closure of $A$ is the union of $A$ and the set $A'$ of all its cluster (limit) points.

solution_steps.title: Smallest Closed Superset
solution_steps.math: \overline{A} = \bigcap \{F \subseteq X : F \text{ is closed and } A \subseteq F\}
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently, $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$.

solution_steps.title: Metric Formulation
solution_steps.math: \overline{A} = \{x \in X : \forall r > 0, \, B(x, r) \cap A \ne \emptyset\}
solution_steps.explanation: All points having distance 0 from $A$.

final_answer: The closure of $A$, denoted $\overline{A}$, is the union of $A$ with all its limit points ($A \cup A'$), which is the smallest closed set containing $A$.
exam_tip: State that $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Show that the intersection of two open sets in a metric space is open.
concept_tested: Intersection of Two Open Sets is Open
approach: Let $x \in U_1 \cap U_2$, choose $r = \min(r_1, r_2) > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Setup
solution_steps.math: x \in U_1 \cap U_2 \implies x \in U_1 \quad \text{and} \quad x \in U_2
solution_steps.explanation: Point belongs to both sets.

solution_steps.title: Open Balls in Each Set
solution_steps.math: \exists r_1 > 0 : B(x, r_1) \subseteq U_1, \qquad \exists r_2 > 0 : B(x, r_2) \subseteq U_2
solution_steps.explanation: Because $U_1$ and $U_2$ are open.

solution_steps.title: Taking Minimum Radius
solution_steps.math: r = \min(r_1, r_2) > 0 \implies B(x, r) \subseteq B(x, r_1) \subseteq U_1 \land B(x, r) \subseteq B(x, r_2) \subseteq U_2
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $B(x, r) \subseteq U_1 \cap U_2$, showing $U_1 \cap U_2$ is open.

final_answer: Since $B(x, \min(r_1, r_2)) \subseteq U_1 \cap U_2$, the intersection is open.
exam_tip: By induction, any finite intersection of open sets is open.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define dense sets in a metric space and give an example.
concept_tested: Dense Sets in Metric Spaces
approach: Define $\overline{A} = X$ or every ball contains points of $A$; give example $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: A \subseteq X \text{ is dense in } (X, d) \iff \overline{A} = X
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently, every non-empty open set in $X$ contains at least one point of $A$ (i.e. $\forall x \in X, \forall r > 0, B(x, r) \cap A \ne \emptyset$).

solution_steps.title: Example
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{Q} \text{ is dense in } \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: Between any two real numbers there exists a rational number (Density Theorem), so $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{R}$.

final_answer: A subset $A$ is dense in $X$ if $\overline{A} = X$. Example: $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$ under the standard metric.
exam_tip: Another example: The irrationals $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$ are also dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define a discrete metric space and verify its metric axioms.
concept_tested: Discrete Metric Space and Metric Axioms
approach: Define $d(x, y) = 0$ if $x=y$ and $1$ if $x \ne y$; verify the 4 axioms.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: d(x, y) = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } x = y \\ 1, & \text{if } x \ne y \end{cases}
solution_steps.explanation: The discrete metric on any non-empty set $X$.

solution_steps.title: Verification of Axioms
solution_steps.math: (1) \, d \ge 0; \quad (2) \, d(x,y)=0 \iff x=y; \quad (3) \, d(x,y)=d(y,x) \text{ (symmetric)}; \quad (4) \, d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)
solution_steps.explanation: For triangle inequality: if $x = z$, $0 \le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ holds trivially. If $x \ne z$, then $y$ cannot equal both $x$ and $z$, so at least one of $d(x,y)$ or $d(y,z)$ is 1, giving $1 \le 1+0=1$ or $1 \le 1+1=2$.

final_answer: The discrete metric is $d(x,y) = 0$ if $x=y$ and $1$ if $x \ne y$. It satisfies all four axioms; in this space every singleton $\{x\} = B(x, 1/2)$ is open.
exam_tip: Mention that in a discrete metric space, every subset of $X$ is both open and closed.

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: Define an isolated point of a subset of a metric space.
concept_tested: Isolated Point of a Subset of a Metric Space
approach: Define isolated point as a point of $A$ which is not a limit point of $A$.

solution_steps.title: Definition
solution_steps.math: x_0 \in A \text{ is an isolated point of } A \iff \exists r > 0 \text{ such that } B(x_0, r) \cap A = \{x_0\}
solution_steps.explanation: An isolated point of $A$ is a point in $A$ around which there is an open ball containing no other points of $A$.

final_answer: $x_0 \in A$ is an isolated point if there exists an open ball $B(x_0, r)$ such that $B(x_0, r) \cap A = \{x_0\}$.
exam_tip: Example: In $A = [0, 1] \cup \{2\}$, the point $2$ is an isolated point (choose $r = 1/2$).

topic: Topic 5: Sequences & Series of Functions, Uniform Convergence
question: State Sequential Criterion for Limits of functions.
concept_tested: Sequential Criterion for Limits of Functions
approach: State $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \iff \forall (x_n) \to c$ ($x_n \ne c$), $f(x_n) \to L$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \iff \left( \forall (x_n) \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}, \; \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = c \implies \lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = L \right)
solution_steps.explanation: A function $f$ has limit $L$ at $c$ if and only if for every sequence $(x_n)$ converging to $c$ (with $x_n \ne c$), the image sequence $f(x_n)$ converges to $L$.

solution_steps.title: Divergence Criterion
solution_steps.math: f \text{ has no limit at } c \iff \exists (x_n), (y_n) \to c \text{ with } \lim f(x_n) \ne \lim f(y_n)
solution_steps.explanation: Finding two sequences with different image limits proves the functional limit does not exist.

final_answer: $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ if and only if for every sequence $(x_n)$ in the domain with $x_n \ne c$ converging to $c$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = L$.
exam_tip: Crucial requirement: $x_n \ne c$ for all $n$ must be specified in the definition.
